title: Trading Bot
tagline: A paper-money trading system that scans stocks, options and crypto, checks every order against hard risk rules, and logs every decision for later grading.
note: Paper trading only: it uses Alpaca's pretend-money account. No real money is involved, and nothing here is investment advice.
problem: I wanted to understand how an automated trading system is actually put together: data in, a decision rule, risk controls, execution, and a record you can audit afterwards. I also wanted to test a practical question: does an AI advisor make better calls than a simple rule? That needs a clean log of every decision, not just the trades.
built:
A Python system that runs itself on a schedule against Alpaca's paper-trading API:

  • Strategy: a moving-average crossover (5-day vs 20-day) across about 70 large US stocks, plus options (long calls and puts only) and 24/7 crypto.
  • Risk engine: a "bouncer" that every order must pass: daily loss limit, trade-count cap, allowed-stock list, max positions, max dollars per stock.
  • Diary: SQLite tables for every run, decision (with its reasoning) and trade.
  • AI advisor: Claude reads prices, signals and news and gives an opinion per stock. It never trades; its calls are only logged and graded.
  • Dashboard: a local multi-page site: overview, holdings, options, crypto, decisions, trades, scoreboard.

steps.title: Connect to the paper account
steps.body: Set up the project, stored the API keys in a .env file that is never committed, and printed the pretend account balance to prove the connection works.

steps.title: Look up prices, then buy and sell one share
steps.body: Fetched live quotes and daily bars, then placed a single market buy and sold it back. This was the smallest possible end-to-end test before any strategy existed.

steps.title: The safety bouncer (risk engine)
steps.body: Before writing any strategy, every order had to ask one function for permission. It answers YES or NO with a reason, and sells are always allowed so the bot can get out of a position.
steps.code:
MAX_DOLLARS_PER_STOCK = 2000
MAX_STOCKS_HELD = 5
MAX_TRADES_PER_DAY = 16
DAILY_LOSS_LIMIT = 500

ok, why = can_i_trade(client, "AAPL", shares=3, price_per_share=230, side="buy")
# -> (False, "NO. We already hold 5 different stocks (limit is 5). Sell something first.")

steps.title: A first rule-based robot
steps.body: A moving-average crossover: buy when the 5-day average moves above the 20-day, sell when it drops back below. It is deliberately simple, so it works as a baseline.

steps.title: A diary of every move
steps.body: Three SQLite tables, runs, decisions and trades, record everything, including WAIT decisions and the reason for each one. Without this, there's nothing to grade later.

steps.title: Run by itself, plus a web dashboard
steps.body: auto_run.py loops during market hours; a local dashboard shows account value, holdings, decisions and trades. Later, macOS LaunchAgents replaced the loop so it runs unattended every 30 minutes for weeks.

steps.title: The AI advisor (advisory only)
steps.body: Claude Haiku reads each stock's recent prices, the crossover signal and news headlines, then answers BUY, SELL or WAIT with a reason. That answer goes into the diary as a separate strategy. It costs about a third of a cent per run.

steps.title: Scoreboard: rule vs AI
steps.body: compare.py lines up every decision against what the price actually did 3 or 5 trading days later, and checks whether either strategy beat simply staying invested.

steps.title: Scan a whole universe of stocks
steps.body: Instead of a handful of tickers, each run scans about 70 large, liquid US stocks, sells anything no longer trending up, and buys the strongest fresh crossovers, up to 5 positions.

steps.title: Options and crypto
steps.body: Options: buy a call on a fresh upward cross or a put on a downward one, one contract at a time. The bot closes at +50%, -50% or 5 days before expiry, and never sells options to open, so the worst case is what was paid. Crypto runs 24/7 on the same crossover idea, with its own smaller limits.

results:
• A working, scheduled system that has paper-traded unattended, logging every run, decision and trade.
  • Every order passes through one auditable risk function, and the limits live in one settings file.
  • The rule-vs-AI scoreboard is in place; the comparison needs weeks of logged decisions before it means anything, so no win-rate is claimed here.
next:
• Once enough history is logged, publish the scoreboard: hit rate and return for each strategy against buy-and-hold.
  • Backtest the crossover rule on several years of data before trusting the live numbers.
  • Replace fixed dollar sizing with volatility-based position sizing.
